w:r.w:t: Passive WiFi CSI Cognitive Health Monitoring
Multi-Evidence Attribution Framework for Multi-Occupant Households

SilentSense™ is a passive, camera-free, wearable-free home health monitoring system that uses WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) to detect early behavioural indicators of cognitive decline in elderly individuals living in multi-occupant households. The system's core innovation is not the sensing technology itself — passive WiFi sensing for vitals and activity is an active commercial and research field — but a multi-evidence attribution framework that allows the system to selectively monitor one named individual (the elderly resident) within a home where multiple people are continuously present, without requiring signal separation, cameras, or wearables on any household member.

Every existing passive WiFi health-monitoring product — including category leaders Cognitive Systems (WiFi Motion) and Electronic Caregiver (Addison Care / Addison Aware) — operates at the household level. They detect that something changed in the home, but cannot attribute that change to a specific person. In any home with more than one occupant, this makes individual health-trend tracking unreliable.

Combine four independent, individually-imperfect evidence sources — spatial containment, temporal scheduling, biometric signature matching, and behavioural context priors — into a single Bayesian confidence score per time window. Only high-confidence windows are used for long-term health trend computation; low-confidence windows are gracefully excluded rather than corrupting the baseline.
Commodity hardware (ESP32-S3 at ~$9, Raspberry Pi 4B at ~$50) now supports CSI extraction that previously required research-grade NICs (Intel 5300) or SDRs (USRP)
A December 2025 Oxford study (VitalCSI) validated contactless respiratory monitoring on fully off-the-shelf hardware with r²=0.93, MAE=1.20 brpm across 6–33 brpm
Active open-source platforms (e.g. RuView/WiFi-DensePose) now provide pretrained models, firmware, and smart-home integrations as reusable building blocks

Two well-funded commercial players (Cognitive Systems, Electronic Caregiver) have validated the market and the camera-free value proposition, but have explicitly left individual attribution in multi-person homes as a roadmap item, not a shipped feature

Cognitive decline develops gradually, over months or years. Families miss early warning signs because elderly individuals often live independently or semi-independently, symptoms accumulate slowly, doctor visits are infrequent (typically annual or semi-annual), and existing monitoring solutions are either too invasive (cameras), too unreliable in long-term compliance (wearables that get forgotten or run out of charge), or too infrequent (periodic medical assessments that cannot observe daily life).

Passive WiFi CSI is a superposition signal: every body in the sensing field reflects and disturbs the WiFi signal simultaneously, and the receiver captures the algebraic sum of all those reflections. There is no inherent mechanism in standard WiFi hardware to attribute signal components to individual people.
The monitoring target (the elderly person) shares the home with family members, children, and occasional caregivers
Health metrics — gait speed, sleep quality, breathing rate, eating patterns, fall events — must be attributed to the correct individual to be clinically meaningful
Unattributed or misattributed data corrupts the long-term behavioural baseline that gives the system its actual value: detecting drift over weeks and months

The SilentSense sensing network is COMPLETELY SEPARATE from the household's internet WiFi router. A dedicated ESP32 or Raspberry Pi TX/RX pair is installed inside the target individual's room, on a private sensing-only network. The home router continues to provide internet only and is never used for health sensing.

6. Core Innovation — The Four-Pillar Attribution Framework

The conventional approach treats multi-person CSI as a signal separation problem: decompose the mixed stream to isolate one person. This is the approach taken by Independent Component Analysis (ICA) and Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) methods, and it is genuinely hard — RuView's own measured result shows cardiac+respiratory channels alone give a similarity gap of only ~0.0005 between two people, i.e. essentially no separation.

SilentSense's reframe: do not separate signals. Instead, build a person-attributed sensing architecture where attribution emerges from converging evidence across four independent channels. No single channel needs to be perfect — the system only needs enough channels to agree, often enough, to build a statistically meaningful baseline.

Both TX and RX nodes are placed inside the target's room, on opposite walls. At 2.4GHz, a standard interior wall attenuates signal by approximately 10–15 dB. Reflections from people in adjacent rooms therefore arrive at roughly 1/10th to 1/30th the power of in-room motion. The room itself becomes a physical spatial filter — the target individual becomes the dominant signal source by physics, not algorithm.
Strength: Highest-confidence pillar; works passively 24/7 with zero compute cost
Limitation: Does not resolve the case where another person physically enters the target's room (e.g. a caregiver, a visiting family member)

A probabilistic daily schedule model is built from weeks of occupancy data (using the shared-space occupancy sensor from Layer 1). The model learns, per hour-of-day and per day-of-week, the probability that the target's room is single-occupant.
Strength: Free — requires no additional hardware beyond the occupancy sensor; overnight (11pm–7am) typically yields 8+ hours of near-certain single-occupancy data every night
Limitation: Breaks down for atypical schedules (irregular caregiver visits, shift-working household members, illness disrupting routine)

During known single-occupant windows (informed by Pillars 1+2), the system builds an enrolled biometric profile for the target individual: a probability distribution over breathing rate, breathing regularity, and breathing amplitude (reconstructed from CSI). During ambiguous daytime windows, the respiratory-band PSD is analysed for multiple frequency peaks; each peak's likelihood under the target's enrolled distribution versus a generic household distribution produces a likelihood ratio.

RuView's own measured result shows breathing-rate-alone separation between two people can be near-zero (gap ~0.0005) when rates overlap. Pillar 3 must therefore use the FULL distribution — rate, regularity, AND amplitude/depth — not a single-value comparison. Elderly breathing differs from younger adults in resting rate (12–16 vs 16–20 brpm), amplitude (reduced chest wall compliance), and irregularity pattern (micro-arousals). Even with all three dimensions, expect Pillar 3 to be probabilistic enrichment, not deterministic separation.
Strength: Extends attributable windows beyond Pillars 1+2 alone, particularly for daytime periods when the target is alone in their room but the household is otherwise active
Limitation: Degrades significantly during motion (breathing signal requires relative stillness); overlapping breathing rates between household members remain a genuine edge case

Uses occupancy-only detection in shared spaces (no identity required there) as a Bayesian prior. If the shared-space sensor shows no activity and the target's room shows motion, the probability that the motion belongs to the target is very high — they are the only person expected to be present when the rest of the household is quiet.
Strength: Requires no identification infrastructure outside the target's room — identity logic stays concentrated where it matters
Limitation: A weak prior on its own; most valuable as a multiplier on the other three pillars

Each pillar contributes an independent probability/confidence score for a given 30-second window. The fusion layer combines these into P(target individual | spatial, temporal, biometric, behavioural). Windows above a confidence threshold are used for health metric computation and baseline updates; windows below threshold are logged as 'household activity period' and excluded — not discarded entirely, but down-weighted in long-term trend analysis.

The four pillars are NOT sequential filters. They are independent evidence sources combined probabilistically. A window only needs to score high on ENOUGH pillars — the system never requires all four to fire simultaneously.

7.5 MVP Delivery Surface — Home Assistant / Matter Integration

Rather than building a custom mobile application at MVP stage, SilentSense leverages RuView's existing Home Assistant integration (MQTT auto-discovery, HAP-1.1 bridge for Apple Home, Matter endpoint for Google Home/Alexa). This provides immediate dashboards, notifications, and entity-level data (presence, vitals, semantic states such as 'elderly-inactivity-anomaly') on infrastructure families may already use, eliminating the custom-app development line item from the MVP timeline entirely.
Phase 1–2: Home Assistant dashboard + push notifications via existing HA mobile apps
Phase 3+: Evaluate custom Flutter app only if HA-based delivery proves insufficient for non-technical family members
